abstract.p: Polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPLs) and perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) are pervasive contaminants of great concern and can enter human body primarily through gastrointestinal tract. However, their single and combined effects on female reproductive health remain poorly explored. In this study, PFBA was found to be adsorbed onto PS-NPLs through both chemical and physical interactions. Compared with single exposure, co-exposure to PS-NPLs (0.04 mg/d) and PFBA (0.28 mg/d) for 28 days caused more severe ovarian toxicity in rats, as evidenced by decreased primordial follicles, increased follicular atresia, and sex hormone abnormalities. Mechanistically, the co-exposure was associated with the gut barrier damage and elevated levels of lipopolysaccharide in the bloodstream, concomitant with altered redox homeostasis, inflammation and NLRP3/caspase-1-related pyroptosis of the ovary. Moreover, supplementation with probiotic Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 partially attenuated ovarian injury via modulating gut microbiota and mitigating the above process. Taken together, our study revealed a synergistic impact of PS-NPLs and PFBA on female reproduction, uncovered the underlying mechanisms from the perspective of gut-ovary axis, and provided valuable insights into potential preventive strategies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The global production of plastics has substantially escalated, amounting to 400.3 million tons in 2022, with projections indicating an exponential increase thereafter [1]. Plastics can be designed to be nanoscale and larger plastics can also break down into smaller particles, including the microplastics (< 5 mm) and nanoplastics (< 1 μm) through weathering and abrasion [2]. Recent clinical evidence has indicated that micro- and nanoplastics may be associated with adverse health outcomes, including endocrine disruption, immune dysregulation, reproductive toxicity, and cardiovascular effects [3, 4]. They can also trigger persistent gastrointestinal inflammation, driving epithelial cell apoptosis and impairing intestinal barrier integrity [5]. Polystyrene (PS), one of the most commonly used plastics and most serious pollutants, is produced through the polymerization of styrene monomers. In vivo and in vitro research have indicated that polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPLs) can build up within the food chain and penetrate organisms via the inhalation, dermal and gastrointestinal absorption [6].

Studies have showed that organic pollutants like per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can be adsorbed onto nanoplastics through chemical (chemisorption) and physical (physisorption) interactions [7, 8]. The co-exposure has been found to enhance the bioavailability and adverse biological effects of the pollutants, which was also referred as the “Trojan horse effect”. For instance, co-exposure of polystyrene microplastics and phenanthrene led to increased phenanthrene accumulation in zebrafish, along with greater oxidative damage and enhanced immune response [9]. One potential reason was attributed to the combined toxicity of the pollutants and nanoplastics on intestine with the physical abrasion and reactive oxygen species (ROS) induction. This caused the thinning of the mucus layer, tight junction reduction, epithelial cell apoptosis and eventually increased permeability of the intestinal barrier [10].

Perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA), a short-chain PFAS increasingly utilized as a replacement for long-chain PFAS, has become ubiquitous in the environment [8, 11]. PFBA is frequently identified in various human specimens, including blood, umbilical cord serum and placental tissue [12]. Previous research has suggested that PFBA may impair reproductive function in certain animal models through disruption of endocrine system such as sex steroid synthesis and estrogen receptor signaling [11, 13]. Analysis of data from the birth cohort study revealed a positive association between the likelihood of preterm birth and the level of PFBA exposure modulated by estrogen [14]. There was also a negative association between sperm motility in males and semen levels of PFBA [15]. However, in vitro experiments with human cells showed that PFBA, along with other PFAS, did not necessarily exhibit anti-androgenic or anti-estrogenic activities, and had minimal effects on the expression of steroidogenic genes [16]. This suggests that PFBA may interfere with reproductive function via other pathways. Recent findings indicate that PFBA may also exert toxicity through the gut, as exposure significantly alters intestinal antioxidant enzyme activity, damages villus morphology, and reduces microbial diversity and community complexity, leading to impaired intestinal barrier function [17]. Such intestinal disturbances are known to influence systemic inflammation and hormonal regulation, suggesting a potential link between PFBA exposure and the gut–ovary axis. To the best of our knowledge, the impact of PFBA on ovarian histopathology and function, as well as the related mechanisms, has not been investigated before. Additionally, no studies have yet explored the impact of co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA.

It has been proposed that the co-exposure to micro-/nano-plastics and other pollutants can induce oxidative stress, inflammation, and consequently cell death [18]. Among them, pyroptosis is a novel form of programmed cell death distinct from apoptosis and necrosis [19]. It is characterized by the formation of pores in the cell membrane, leading to cell swelling, lysis, and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, thereby exacerbating tissue damage. In the canonical pathway, Toll-Like Receptor (TLR) signals (e.g., lipopolysaccharide [LPS] binding to TLR), death signals (e.g., FasR-FasL interaction) or inflammation (e.g., IL-1β or TNF-α sensing) can trigger NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) expression. Subsequently, oxidative, ionic or physical stresses can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, a critical component in the initiation of pyroptosis [19, 20]. The NLRP3 inflammasome, upon activation, recruits and activates caspase-1, a protease responsible for cleaving the gasdermin-D (GSDMD) protein and the maturation of IL-1β and IL-18. Cleaved GSDMD forms pores in the cell membrane, further facilitating the release of the pro-inflammatory cytokines [21]. In previous research, pyroptosis has been involved in a variety of ovarian diseases, including premature ovarian insufficiency, polycystic ovary syndrome and ovarian aging [22].

Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 is a probiotic strain isolated from traditional Chinese fermented foods. Previous research demonstrated that P101 alleviates alcohol-induced testicular dysfunction and alcoholic liver injury through regulating the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant pathway [23, 24]. P101 has also shown significant potential in mitigating environmental pollutant-induced bone injury through restoring intestinal microbial homeostasis and inhibiting inflammatory response [25]. Furthermore, Yuan et al. revealed the effects of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum on oxidative stress and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in broiler breast meat [26]. Building on these findings, we hypothesized that P101 might uniquely block the “priming” and “activation” signals of the NLRP3/caspase-1 pyroptotic pathway, thereby providing a novel strategy to alleviate the synergistic reproductive toxicity of PS-NPLs and PFBA via the gut-ovary axis.

This study aimed to (1) investigate the single and combined toxicological effects of PFBA and PS-NPLs on ovarian tissue, (2) elucidate the underlying mechanisms of the reproductive toxicity focusing on the gut-ovary axis and pyroptosis, and (3) explore whether probiotic Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 supplementation can ameliorate ovarian pyroptosis through regulating intestinal barrier. For the first time, these findings not only provide a foundational understanding on the impact of PFBA and PS-NPLs exposure in mammal ovaries but also offer critical insights for developing strategies to mitigate the combined reproductive toxicity.

sec.title: Characterization of PS-NPLs and PFBA
sec.p: The PS-NPLs suspensions (1.645 g/ml) with a particle size of 100 nm were sourced from Baseline ChromTech Research Center (Tianjin, China). The selected small size can translocate within the body easily and induce greater toxicity [27]. PFBA (25 mg/ml; CAS#: 375-22−4) was provided by MedChemExpress (New Jersey, USA). For sample preparation, solution of PS-NPLs, PFBA, and PS-NPLs mixed with PFBA were dropped on aluminized flakes and air-dried. The size and morphology of the PS-NPLs and PFBA/PS-NPLs were characterized via field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Sigma 300, Zeiss, Germany). The zeta potential of the PS-NPLs, PFBA, and PFBA/PS-NPLs in the water were measured by Zetasizer (Nano ZS90, Malvern Panalytical, UK). Additionally, the internal structure, chemical bonds, and molecular vibration patterns were characterized by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR; Thermos Scientific, USA).

sec.title: Experimental animals and design
sec.p: The study utilized sexually mature female Sprague-Dawley rats, approximately 7 weeks old, supplied by Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, China. Ethical approval for the experiments was granted by the Animal Care Review Committee of Nanchang University (Approval No. 0064257), adhering to guidelines for animal welfare. The certificate of ethical approval is available upon request. Rats were acclimated for one week in the lab with access to clean water, food, stable temperature and humidity, and a 12-hour light/dark cycle.

The rats were randomly divided into four groups (8 rats per group): control, PFBA (0.28 mg/d), PS-NPLs (0.04 mg/d), and PN co-exposure (0.28 mg/d PFBA + 0.04 mg/d PS-NPLs). Sample size calculations were performed a priori using G*Power 3.1. The analysis of eight mice per group was based on an anticipated 25% difference in mean antral follicle counts with a 20% standard deviation, yielding 80% power at α = 0.05. The control group received uncontaminated physiological saline only. The PS-NPLs group was administered 200 µL of PS-NPLs solution (0.2 mg/mL) daily by gavage, and the PFBA group received 200 µL of PFBA solution (1.4 mg/mL) daily. For the PN co-exposure group, PS-NPLs and PFBA were premixed at their respective concentrations (0.2 mg/mL PS-NPLs and 1.4 mg/mL PFBA) and co-administered once daily in a single 200 µL gavage to ensure simultaneous exposure without additional handling stress. Dosing was calculated based on actual human environmental exposure and also consistent with prior studies [28–32].

To evaluate the protective effect of probiotic treatment, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 was used in this research. The safety, efficacy, and dosing of this strain have been evaluated in our previous studies through both in vivo and in vitro experiments [23, 24]. The strain was incubated at 37 °C for 16 h to achieve a bacterial density of 108 CFU/mL. Twenty-four female rats were randomly allocated into three groups (8 rats per group): control, PN and PN+P101. The control group received physiological saline, while the two other experimental groups were treated with PN as described above. For probiotic administration, the culture of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 and MRS broth was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 2 min at 24 °C. The supernatant was removed, and the bacterial pellet was washed and re-suspended in 1% PBS. Rats in the PN+P101 group were then supplemented with 200 µL of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 suspension orally, administered half an hour after the PN mixture gavage.

For all groups, the weights of rats were recorded daily. After 28 days, rats were euthanized for organs and blood sample collection. Specimens of blood and organs were stored at −80 °C for further analysis.

sec.title: Histopathological analysis
sec.p: The ovarian and intestinal tissues were excised from the rats, and promptly immersed in 4% paraformaldehyde fixative. Prior to paraffin embedding, the tissues underwent a dehydration process with gradient concentrations of ethanol. Sections of 5 μm thickness were cut from the paraffin blocks and subjected to hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) or alcian blue-periodic acid-schiff (AB-PAS) staining. Following staining, the sections were sealed with the neutral resin.

For microscopic examination, the Ti optical microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan) was utilized to capture images of the tissue sections. From each tissue block, one section was selected every 50 μm, and three representative sections per animal were analyzed. The histopathological assessment of the ovaries focused on the enumeration of growing (primary, secondary, and antral) and atretic follicles. The criteria for follicle staging, as defined by Pascuali et al. with slight adaptations, were applied: primordial follicles were identified by a single layer of flattened (squamous) granulosa cells around the oocyte; primary follicles by a single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells around the oocyte; secondary follicles by two or more layers without an antral cavity; antral follicles by the presence of an antral space; and atretic follicles by the presence of degenerating oocytes or pyknotic granulosa cells [33]. Histology score of the colons was determined according to a previously established scoring system shown as follows: crypt destruction (0–4 scale), degree of inflammation (0–3 scale), and depth of damage (0–3 scale) [34]. Two independent evaluators blinded to group allocation performed the follicle counting and histological scoring to minimize bias.

sec.title: Biochemical analysis
sec.p: The 10% ovarian protein homogenate was prepared using physiological saline, and the protein concentrations were measured using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit (Applygen, Beijing, China). Commercial kits (Jiancheng Bioengineering, Nanjing, China) were utilized to assess antioxidant enzyme activities. Catalase (CAT) activity was determined by the visible light molybdate method (A007-1-1), superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity was quantified by the WST-1 method (A001-3-2) and total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) was measured using the ABTS method (A015-2-1). ELISA kits (Yiyan Biological Technology, Shanghai, China) were used to evaluate serum levels of LPS (YS-SN605) and sex hormones, including estradiol (E2) (YS-NC1168), progesterone (P) (YS-SNM553), and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) (YS-MN3185). All procedures were conducted according to the manufacturers’ instructions.

sec.title: Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR)
sec.p: Adhering to the procedures described in prior research [35], we extracted the total RNA using the RNA extraction kit (Axygen Scientific, San Francisco, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and determined its concentration. Total RNA was reverse transcribed it into cDNA by PrimeScript TM RT reagent kit (Cat#RR047A, Lot#AK2802, Takara, Kusatsu, Japan). Subsequently, RT-qPCR analysis was performed on Real-Time PCR System (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA, USA) using TB Green Premix (Cat#RR820A, Takara). The 2−ΔΔCt approach was then applied to attain the RT-qPCR results. β-actin served as the internal control gene, and the corresponding primer sequences were listed in Table S1. Tsingke Biological Technology (Beijing, China) synthesized all the primers.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
sec.p: The IHC assay was conducted to assess the expression of TLR4, NLRP3, Caspase-1, GSDMD, IL-1β and IL-18 in ovary, as well as Mucin 2 (MUC2) and Occludin in colon. Initially, tissue sections embedded in paraffin were deparaffinized and rehydrated. Next, the sections underwent antigen retrieval, endogenous peroxidase blocking, and serum blocking. Primary antibody incubation was then performed with specific antibodies: TLR4 (1:1000, Catalog#: GB 11519), NLRP3 (1:200, Catalog#: GB 114320), Caspase-1 (1:1000, Catalog#: GB 11383), GSDMD (1:500, Catalog#: WL 05686), IL-1β (1:500, Catalog#: GB 11113), and IL-18 (1:500, Catalog#: GB 115632), MUC2 (1:1000, Catalog#: GB 11344), and Occludin (1:500, Catalog#: GB 111401). Subsequently, the sections underwent secondary antibody incubation, DAB chromogenic reaction, nuclear counterstaining and mounting. All materials for the IHC assays were sourced from Wuhan Servicebio Technology Co., Ltd. (Hubei, China). The IHC results were quantified using ImageJ software (version 6.0, NIH, USA) with the open-source IHC Profiler plugin for automated digital analysis of DAB-stained sections, as described by Varghese et al. [36]. Specifically, pixel intensities (0–255) were divided into predefined ranges: high positive (0–60), positive (61–120), low positive (121–180), and negative (181–235), whereas pixels > 235 were excluded as background. The percentage of pixels within each zone was calculated, and a numerical score was automatically generated from the pixel distribution. When ≥ 66.6% of pixels fell within a single zone, the image was directly assigned to that category; otherwise, a weighted composite score based on zone proportions was computed. The mean IHC score for each sample was obtained from six randomly selected high-power fields.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: Ovarian samples were washed with ice-cold PBS, cut into small fragments, and lysed in modified Radio Immunoprecipitation Assay (RIPA, P0013B, Beyotime, China) containing protease/phosphatase inhibitors (5872 S, Cell Signaling Technology, MA, USA). Homogenates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and protein concentrations in the supernatant were determined using a BCA kit (Servicebio). Equal protein amounts were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE gels and transferred to PVDF membranes (0.45 μm). After blocking with 5% milk in TBS for 30 min, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with antibodies against Caspase-11 [1:1000; Abcam], GSDMD [1:1000; Abcam] or GAPDH [1:10,000, Proteintech]. Horseradish peroxidase-linked secondary antibody [1:2000, Proteintech]). were applied for 30 min, and signals were detected using enzyme chemiluminescence (ECL; Servicebio). Band densities were analyzed with ImageJ software (version 6.0, NIH, USA).

sec.title: TUNEL assay
sec.p: The ovarian paraffin-embedded section was processed by deparaffinization and rehydration, followed by antigen retrieval, permeabilization and equilibration. Subsequently, The TUNEL reaction mixture, consisting of TDT enzyme, dUTP, and buffer in a 1:5:50 ratio, was added to the tissue and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Subsequently, the sections were stained with DAPI to visualize the cell nuclei, followed by washing and sealing with an anti-fade mounting medium. The images were captured at 200× magnification under a fluorescence microscope, and the quantification of TUNEL-positive (red) cells was carried out using ImageJ 6.0. On each slide, the number of positive cells of five randomly selected fields was counted and further averaged per animal. The necessary reagents for TUNEL assays were sourced from Wuhan Servicebio Technology Co., Ltd. (Hubei, China).

sec.title: 16 S rRNA sequencing and analysis
sec.p: Fresh fecal pellets of the control, PN exposure and PN+P101 groups (n = 4 per group) were collected aseptically, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at − 80 °C. Total DNA was extracted and then the V3–V4 region of the 16 S rRNA gene was amplified using primers 338 F and 806R. Amplicons were purified, quantified, and homogenized, and paired-end 300 bp sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq platform. The sequencing data were processed and analyzed through a professional bioinformatics service platform (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) to evaluate alterations in gut microbial composition.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The experimental data were presented as mean with standard deviations. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26.0 (SPSS, Inc., Chicago, Illinois). Normality was assessed separately for each group using Quantile–Quantile (Q–Q) plots and Shapiro–Wilk tests. Homogeneity of variance was evaluated by Levene’s test. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted for group comparisons, followed by the least significant difference (LSD) test when variances were homogeneous (P ≥ 0.05) or Dunnett’s T3 test when variances were unequal (P < 0.05). Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05.

sec.title: Characterization of PS-NPLs and PFBA interaction
sec.p: As shown in the SEM (Fig. 1A), the PS-NPLs were in spherical shape with relatively good dispersion. However, after being mixed with PFBA, the adhesion appeared between the particles (Fig. 1B). The zeta potential of PNs were also significantly lower than that of PS-NPLs, further indicating the decreased dispersion after mixture (Fig. 1C). In infrared spectroscopic analysis (Fig. 1D), the stretching vibration absorption peaks for carbon-oxygen (C-O) and ether (C-O-C) bonds remained at 1082.4 cm⁻¹, while the bending vibration absorption peaks for the = C-H double bond and the C-H bending vibrations in the benzene ring were consistently observed at 962.8 and 925.3 cm⁻¹, respectively. However, a prominent hydroxyl absorption peak at 3369.1 cm⁻¹ appeared in the PN group, indicating the presence of free hydroxyl groups. Furthermore, the carbonyl absorption peak shifted to a lower wavenumber, from 1769.6 to 1638.3 cm⁻¹, suggesting the formation of an n-π conjugation between the n-electrons of the auxiliary chromophore and the π-electrons of the carbonyl group. Additionally, the infrared absorption peaks at 695.5 and 536 cm⁻¹ in the PN group exhibited a red shift indicative of conjugation. The introduction of the auxiliary chromophore, along with the solvation effect, could contribute to the observed shift of the C-H absorption peaks in the aromatic ring toward longer wavelengths. Based on these findings, we speculated that PS-NPLs and PFBA could interact through both chemical and physical routes.

sec.title: Co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA impaired ovarian reserve
sec.p: Following a 28-day exposure period, the rat body weight increased continuously, and the growth rate was similar across groups (Fig. 2A). Ovarian coefficients of the three exposure groups displayed a downwards trend in contrast to the control group, but did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 2B). Histopathological evaluation revealed that the PN co-exposure group had a decreased number of primordial follicles relative to the control group, and a higher count of atretic follicles in comparison with PFBA or PS-NPLs alone (Fig. 2C and D). Serum E2 showed no statistically significant change among groups, whereas progesterone was increased and AMH was reduced in the PN co-exposure group, further suggesting the synergistic impairment of ovarian reserve (Fig. 2E-G).

sec.title: Co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA induced redox imbalance, inflammatory responses and impaired intestinal barrier integrity
sec.p: Micro-/nano-plastics exposure combined with other pollutants often disrupts redox balance and promotes inflammation, resulting in cellular and tissue damage. Therefore, we detected and quantified the enzymatic activity of antioxidant substances (CAT, SOD and T-AOC) and the expression level of inflammation factors (TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-10) in ovarian tissue. The CAT activities were decreased after exposure to nanoplastics and exacerbated in the PN co-exposure group. Contrary to PS-NPLs or PFBA alone, only PN co-exposure led to the significant reduction of SOD and T-AOC activity (Fig. 2I-K). Gene expression levels further validated the downregulated mRNA levels of SOD2 and glutathione peroxidase 1 (GPX1) after co-exposure, while no significant differences were observed in single exposure groups (Fig. 2H). As for inflammation-related cytokines, the expression of pro-inflammatory genes TNF-α and IL-6 were increased, while the expression of anti-inflammatory gene IL-10 was reduced in the PN co-exposure group compared with the control group. This contrasted with the nanoplastic-exposed group, where only the increase in TNF-α expression reached statistical significance, and the PFBA group, where IL-6 expression was the only statistically significant elevation observed (Fig. 3A-C).

sec.p: ROS and inflammation can be induced by LPS through TLR4, the key receptor responsible for LPS recognition and signal initiation [37–39]. Our results further revealed that both PS-NPLs and PN co-exposure elevated the serum LPS levels (Fig. 3D). Accordingly, ovarian IHC staining together with qPCR analysis revealed a significant increase in TLR4 expression following exposure to PFBA, PS-NPLs, and their combination (Fig. 3E and F).

The disruption of the intestinal barrier, followed by the absorption of pollutants and LPS into body, may contribute to their toxic effects on reproduction. Herein, histopathological assessments revealed that exposure to PS-NPLs or PFBA resulted in disorganized and deformed crypt structure, accompanied by mild epithelial disruption. The co-exposure further exacerbated these lesions, showing marked crypt atrophy, epithelial shedding and inflammatory infiltration, indicating a synergistic effect (Fig. 3G). Although AB-PAS staining showed no significant difference in overall mucin intensity, local staining variations and distinct distribution differences were observed (Fig. 3H). In the control group, AB-PAS staining was strong and evenly distributed along the crypt surface, whereas the PN group exhibited weaker and discontinuous staining. MUC2, a protein secreted by epithelial goblet cells, is a key component of the intestinal mucus layer [40]. IHC analysis of MUC2 indicated that the intestinal mucus levels were reduced in PFBA and PS-NPLs groups, and reached the lowest in co-exposure group (Fig. 3I). Similarly, staining of tight junction protein Occludin showed a continuous apical pattern in the control group, which became disrupted and significantly diminished after combined exposure (Fig. 3J).

sec.title: Co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA induced enhanced NLRP3–related pyroptotic signaling in the ovary
sec.p: In the canonical pathway, the NLRP3 inflammasome can be induced by LPS and subsequently activated by oxidative stress. To explore whether co-exposure is accompanied by alterations in this signaling axis, we quantified the gene and protein expression levels of NLRP3, which significantly upregulated following co-exposure to PFBA and PS-NPLs compared with individual treatments. IHC staining showed that NLRP3 immunoreactivity was weak in the control group, slightly enhanced after PFBA or PS-NPLs exposure, and strongly intensified in the co-exposure group (Fig. 4A and B). We then assessed the expression of key downstream effectors in the pyroptosis pathway. qPCR results revealed that the co-exposure caused more obvious increase in the levels of caspase-1, GSDMD, IL-1β and IL-18 than individual exposure (Fig. 4A). Their staining intensity and positive cell area were also minimal in the control, moderately increased in the single-exposure groups, and reached the highest levels with PN co-exposure (Fig. 4B). Consistently, Western blot analysis showed that the protein levels of cleaved GSDMD and caspase-11 were elevated in the PN co-exposure group compared with the PFBA or PS-NPLs single-exposure groups (Fig. 4C). Consequently, the combined exposure group displayed the most pronounced increase in TUNEL-positive cells (Fig.S1).

sec.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 attenuated ovarian impairment and intestinal integrity following PFBA and PS-NPLs co-exposure
sec.p: To validate the role of gut-ovary axis in PS-NPLs and PFBA co-exposure, we applied probiotic treatment with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 for further rescue. The body weight and ovarian organ coefficient of the three groups were similar (Fig. 5A and B). However, histological evaluation revealed that the ovarian structure in the PN+P101 group exhibited improvement compared with the PN group, with a significant decrease in atretic follicles, increase in primordial follicles and more intact follicular walls (Fig. 5C and D). Further investigation into the reproductive hormones also indicated that the changes in P and AMH levels under PN co-exposure were partially restored after P101 supplementation while the change in E2 was not significant (Fig. 5E-G). Moreover, P101 significantly increased ovarian CAT levels and showed a trend towards elevating SOD and T-AOC levels (Fig. 5I-K), which were consistent with the upregulated SOD2 and CAT gene expression (Fig. 5H). P101 also reduced ovarian TNF-α and IL-6 while elevating IL-10 mRNA levels (Fig. 6A-C).

sec.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 mitigated NLRP3-related ovarian pyroptosis
sec.p: We further investigated the impact of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 on LPS-associated ovarian pyroptosis. Following PN co-exposure, the levels of NLRP3 inflammasome and its recruited caspase-1 were significantly elevated, while supplementation with P101 partially attenuated these elevations (Fig. 7A and B). A similar trend was observed for GSDMD, IL-1β, and IL-18, whose staining intensity was attenuated after P101 supplementation (Fig. 7B). Consistent with the IHC results, RT-qPCR results further validated that P101 repressed the co-exposure-induced upregulation of pyroptosis-associated genes, without full normalization to control levels (Fig. 7A). Western blot analysis also showed that the protein levels of cleaved GSDMD and caspase-11 were elevated in the PN co-exposure group but significantly reduced following Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 treatment (Fig. 7C). The TUNEL-positive cells in ovarian tissues were significantly reduced by P101 treatment as well (Fig. S2).

sec.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 modulated gut microbiota following PFBA and PS-NPLs co-exposure
sec.p: To investigate the impact of co-exposure to PFBA and PS-NPLs on gut microbial structure and the restorative effect of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101, 16 S rRNA sequencing was performed. Co-exposure significantly altered the gut microbiota with decreased α-diversity, as indicated by lower Ace index (Fig. 8A) and increased Simpson index (Fig. 8B), reflecting reduced species richness. β-diversity analysis using principal component analysis (PCA) and principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) (Fig. 8C and D) further revealed distinct community separation in the PN group, while Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 supplementation restored the microbial profile toward that of the control group. The number of shared operational taxonomic units (OTUs) increased from 243 (Control vs. PN) to 281 (Control vs. PN + P101) (Fig. 8E), suggesting partial recovery of microbial diversity following probiotic treatment. At the phylum level, co-exposure decreased the relative abundance of Bacteroidota and increased Pseudomonadota (Fig. 8F). LEfSe analysis and cladogram visualization (Fig. 8G and H) identified Lactobacillales and Lactobacillaceae as differentially abundant taxa, which additionally supported Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 intervention. At the class level, the abundance of Clostridia and Coriobacteriia decreased, whereas Elusimicrobia increased significantly under the co-exposure but partially restored after P101 treatment (Fig. 8I-K).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: PS-NPLs are environmentally ubiquitous and can enter the systemic circulation through ingestion and inhalation, raising significant concerns regarding their potential impact on reproductive health [41]. Organic pollutants such as PFBA often engage in physical and chemical interactions with nanoplastics [7, 8]. However, the reproductive toxicity of co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA have not been explored, and the underlying mechanisms require further investigation. Moreover, the imperceptibility of contaminant exposure necessitates the urgent development of preventive strategies. Our results indicated that the co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA resulted in enhanced ovarian toxicity compared with exposure to PS-NPLs or PFBA alone. Under co-exposure, the intestinal barrier was compromised, leading to increased levels of LPS in the bloodstream. In the ovary, LPS could be recognized by TLR4, potentially triggering oxidative imbalance and inflammation. Furthermore, LPS exposure was associated with upregulation of the NLRP3/caspase-1-related pyroptotic markers, suggesting a possible involvement of the gut–ovary axis. Supplementation with probiotic showed potential in mitigating the damage caused by co-exposure, including improving the impaired intestinal barrier, partially normalizing the elevated systemic LPS levels, and ultimately suppressing the pyroptosis in the ovary. This suggested that the probiotic could serve as a potential adjunct strategy to partially alleviate ovarian damage under co-exposure conditions (Fig. 9).

The co-exposure compromised the intestinal barrier, leading to increased levels of LPS in the bloodstream. In the ovary, LPS was recognized by TLR4 and was associated with redox imbalance, inflammation, and NLRP3/caspase-1-related pyroptotic pathway. Probiotic supplementation (P101) mitigated these effects by improving the intestinal barrier, reducing systemic LPS levels, and attenuating pyroptosis in the ovary

sec.p: Consistent with these findings, previous studies have shown that individual exposure to microplastics or PFAS exposure can impair ovarian function, leading to disrupted folliculogenesis, altered sex hormone levels, and reduced fertility [42–44]. However, evidence regarding the combined effects of microplastics and PFAS remains limited, despite reports of their co-occurrence in environmental matrices and even in human breast milk due to mutual adsorption [45–47]. Our study provided new evidence that co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA aggravated ovarian injury, resulting in more severe toxicity than that observed under individual exposures. The exacerbation of ovarian toxicity under the co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA was manifested as decreased primordial follicles, increased follicular atresia, and endocrine abnormalities. In addition, elevated progesterone in the PN group suggested disrupted luteal function and altered steroidogenic regulation [48]. Consistent with this, decreased AMH, a marker closely correlated with the pool of small growing follicles, further supports compromised ovarian reserve under co-exposure [49]. This suggested a synergistic “Trojan horse effect”, which can be attributed to the interaction between the two substances, as well as their combined impact on disrupting the intestinal barrier. On one hand, structural changes post-mixing revealed that fluorine ions from PFBA may react with the benzene rings on PS-NPLs, leading to PFBA adsorption onto PS-NPLs surface with this chemical bonding. The hydrophobic nature of PFBA and the high surface-to-volume ratio of PS-NPLs also contributed to PFBA concentration on PS-NPLs [10]. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that PFAS mixtures can adsorb onto PS-microplastics under environmental conditions, with the aromatic rings of PS monomers aiding in stabilizing the adsorption between PS and PFASs [50]. Therefore, PS-NPLs could act as carriers for PFBA, increasing PFBA accumulation within the body. On the other hand, co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA resulted in more severe damage to the intestinal barrier than individual exposures, as evidenced by the reduced mucus secretion and decreased tight junctions. The intestinal tract is the primary selective absorptive organ, and its integrity is crucial as the first line of defense against external threats [10]. Compromised barrier integrity allowed increased entry of endotoxins and pollutants into the systemic circulation and eventually into organs such as the ovaries, exacerbating the damage through the gut-ovary axis [51]. Although circulating LPS is expected to be very low under physiological conditions, low but quantifiable levels of LPS in rat serum have been reported in prior studies [52, 53]. As evidenced by the elevated serum LPS levels, the increased intestinal permeability under co-exposure allowed more LPS produced by bacteria in the intestinal lumen to enter the bloodstream. Zhang et al. also found that co-exposure to TiO2 nanoparticles and PS-NPLs exacerbated the disruption of the intestinal barrier, leading to increased translocation of TiO2 NPs to the ovaries, which ultimately resulted in aggravated reproductive toxicity [54].

We also observed alterations in the gut microbiota induced by PFBA and PS-NPLs co-exposure, providing further evidence for the involvement of the gut-ovary axis. At the phylum level, the co-exposure lead to the reduction in the relative abundance of Bacteroidota, which can impair hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal signaling [55], and in turn affects the secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. The increased abundance of Pseudomonadota has been implicated in alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism [56], while the decrease of Clostridia under co-exposure is correlated with of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α) secretion [57]. Coriobacteriiais have been proven to be an essential defense mechanism against gut microbiota dysbiosis [58], and its decreased abundance also contributes to inflammation and cognitive impairment [59, 60]. These microbial alterations are consistent with the hormonal disturbances and inflammatory responses observed in our study.

Previous studies have reported that nanoplastics can impair mitochondrial function and disrupt inter-organelle communication, thereby enhancing oxidative stress, disturbing calcium homeostasis, reducing ATP production, and triggering cellular stress responses such as mitophagy and apoptosis [61]. Our findings further identified that LPS-mediated pyroptosis could be another potential mechanism contributing to cellular damage. PS-NPLs exposure has been demonstrated to perturb the gut microbiota, which could increase the production of LPS, a component on the outer surface of Gram-negative bacteria [62]. The elevated serum LPS levels and the upregulation of TLR4 in the ovaries observed in this study suggest that LPS could circulate to the ovary and activate TLR4 signaling, thereby contributing to the altered redox homeostasis and inflammatory responses detected in ovarian tissues. Notably, ovarian TLR4 mRNA was significantly increased only in the PN group, whereas IHC suggested broader protein-level changes across exposure groups. This discrepancy is not unexpected, as mRNA abundance does not necessarily parallel protein expression. Translational regulation, protein stability and turnover, as well as post-transcriptional control of TLR4 have all been reported to uncouple transcription from protein accumulation [63, 64]. In addition, IHC offers a semi-quantitative and spatially resolved assessment of protein distribution within specific cell populations, which is sensitive to localized changes but may not strictly mirror bulk transcriptional alterations, thereby introducing an inherent methodological limitation that should be interpreted in conjunction with transcriptional and biochemical data. In alignment with this study’s observations, parallel research has similarly revealed that LPS significantly increased ROS levels in porcine and bovine oocytes, along with a decreased expression of genes coding for antioxidant enzymes (SOD2, CAT, and GPX1) [65]. Additionally, the activation of TLR4 by LPS stimulated a cascade of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Bromfield and Sheldon found that these cytokines accumulated in bovine ovarian cortex culture supernatants in a LPS concentration-dependent manner [66]. Regarding pyroptosis, it has been identified as a contributing factor to various ovarian disorders and reproductive diseases. The canonical pathway entails a two-step process involving the initiation/priming and subsequent activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome [21]. Specifically, LPS acted as a danger signal by binding to TLR4, which mediated downstream signaling through MyD88 and TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF) proteins. This led to the activation of the transcription factor NF-κB, resulting in the induction of NLRP3 transcription. Additionally, the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α can also activate the NF-κB pathway via TRAF and jointly initiate the priming of NLRP3. In addition to the priming process, the NLRP3 activation necessitates an “activation” signal, one of which is the production of ROS [20]. Following inflammasome assembly, the NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD signaling pathway is activated and mature IL-1β and IL-18 are released through the GSDMD-formed nonselective pores [67]. This excessive stimulation further exacerbates pathological inflammation, creating a feedback loop that perpetuated tissue damage [68]. The activation of NLRP3 was implicated in the disruption of follicular functions, the development of ovarian fibrosis, and reduced ovarian reserve [69], which were consistent with our present finding. In addition to the canonical pathway, the possible involvement of non-canonical pyroptotic signaling cannot be excluded. In the present study, increased caspase-11 expression in the PN co-exposure group provided preliminary suggestion of an associated molecular change. However, it should be noted that caspase-11 is a well-established cytosolic LPS sensor primarily in mice, and rats are not considered a validated model for caspase-11–dependent non-canonical inflammasome activation.

Given the ovarian damage caused by the combined exposure of PS-NPLs and PFBA via the gut-ovary axis, we supplemented probiotic to investigate its protective effect against ovarian injury under such exposure. Prior studies have demonstrated that Lactiplantibacillus plantarum 101 possessed robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, alleviating liver injury as well as testicular dysfunction [23, 70] Consistently, our findings showed significant differences in antioxidant enzymatic activity and the expression level of inflammation-related factors between the PN and the PN+P101 groups. These effects could be attributed to the probiotic functions, including the modulation of gut microbiota structure and the improvement of intestinal barrier function observed in this study [23, 70]. Moreover, emerging evidence suggests that probiotics can exert direct antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects through the production of metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), whose key amino-acid residues may interact with the TLR4/MD-2 complex, MyD88, and NF-κB signaling pathways to exert inhibitory effect [71]. These, in turn, helped to inhibit LPS-induced pyroptosis and partially protect against ovarian structural and functional damage. After supplementation with probiotic, the ovarian tissue exposed to PN showed an increase in primordial follicles and a decrease in atretic follicles. Additionally, AMH, the key marker of ovarian reserve, exhibited significant alleviation [72]. These findings suggested that probiotics may represent a potential adjunct strategy to mitigate the toxic effects of PS-NPLs and PFBA exposure. However, given the environmental exposure variability in real world, clinical evidence should be further explored regarding the human dose equivalence as well as the feasibility, efficiency, and long-term safety of probiotic interventions.

This study has several limitations to address. Firstly, building on previous literature that nanoplastics exposure leads to activation of mitophagy and apoptosis [61], our findings further suggest that pyroptosis may represent an additional cell death pathway. However, the potential involvement of other death mechanisms cannot be fully excluded and warrants further investigation. Secondly, the exposure levels of PS-NPLs and PFBA in the intestinal, blood and ovarian tissues should be measured to better understand their bioavailability, though accurate detection remains challenging due to their low levels [73]. Thirdly, although the upregulation of caspase-11 suggests possible participation of the non-canonical pyroptosis pathway, its precise role and downstream mechanisms require further clarification via species-appropriate models. Moreover, while our data suggest the association between LPS–TLR4 signaling and ovarian pyroptotic responses, future studies incorporating pathway-specific interventions, such as TLR4 inhibition, will help to further refine and substantiate the causal relationships within this axis. Lastly, the effects of different doses and particle sizes of PS-NPLs and PFBA, as well as the minimum effective dose of P101 supplementation need to be explored in our future work.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, our study revealed a synergistic toxic effect of co-exposure to PS-NPLs and PFBA on the ovary. The co-exposure exacerbated the intestinal barrier damage, resulting in elevated levels of LPS in the bloodstream, which in turn promoted ovarian redox imbalance, inflammation and pyroptosis. Furthermore, supplementation with probiotic Lactiplantibacillus plantarum P101 can alleviate the above process to a certain extent. Overall, this work uncovered the underlying mechanisms of the synergistic toxicity of PS-NPLs and PFBA co-exposure from the perspective of the gut-ovary axis, and provided insights into potential mitigation strategies.
